newsitem.title: USA: Hedging seen often vital, especially for smallfry.
newsitem.headline: Hedging seen often vital, especially for smallfry.

text.p: Hedging is a necessary way of controlling financial risk in the energy industry, particularly for smallfry companies, executives told an energy conference Thursday.

"A number of observers have concluded that their firms should not hedge, however this conclusion may be incorrect," Philip Verleger, an economist with Charles River Associates Inc, said at the annual Herold's Pacesetters Energy Conference here.
"Risk management is a tool that may have value to corporate managers and may add to shareholder value. The key is to use the tool correctly," the Washington-based economist said.
Verleger and other executives in the commodity derivatives industry stressed that a number of hedging debacles of the past few years have scared off potential participants in the marketplace.
The misbegotten hedges included substantial losses in 1994 at the U.S. unit of Metallgesellschaft AG and massive copper trading losses disclosed earlier this year at Sumitomo Corp.
Verleger and others acknowledged there was a periously deep potential downside in cases of ill-conceived derivatives risk management.
"When it's not done correctly anything can happen," said Peter Dupre, director of derivatives marketing at Phibro Inc, a subsidiary of Salomon Inc
But when done correctly hedging can be a lifesaver, particularly for small, more financially vulnerable companies, Dupre and others said.
Verleger noted Triton Energy's use of a hedge to pay for an investment in Colombia as one noteworthy example of sound risk management.
"Triton's swap stands as one of the most innovative and attractive examples of the use of hedging in energy markets," Verleger said.

"In this transaction, Triton swapped over 10 million barrels of oil with an investment bank, receiving a cash payment," he said, noting the money was used to pay for Triton's share of the pipeline built to move Cusiana crude from Colombia to the Gulf of Mexico.
By hedging, or locking in prices for its oil, Verleger said Triton averted the risk of having to give up all or part of its stake in the mammoth Cusiana field had oil prices collapsed.
Executives said that while huge companies have the wherewithal to choose whether or not to hedge, for many small companies it is vital insurance.

Verleger said Triton's hedging play in Colombia met with approval from shareholders because the company was thought to be too small to finance its investment in the pipeline without hedging, Verleger said.
"When one looks to hedge, one should have a very clear sense of what kind of (financial) exposure you have," said Charles Adams, vice president of Morgan Stanley in New York.
"Risk management markets are alive and well," he said.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk 212 859-1620
